title: Ideas Are Food
why: English treats ideas as things we cook, serve, taste and digest. Knowing the system lets you describe how good an idea is, how hard it is to accept and how it is presented.
know: the conceptual metaphor IDEAS ARE FOOD and its everyday traces
eight common food idioms for thinking, accepting and teaching
understand: why we digest information and call a weak plan half-baked
which idioms praise, criticise or simply describe
able: evaluate ideas and proposals with precise, idiomatic language
criticise tactfully, for example a plan that is half-baked or news that is hard to swallow
avoid common distortions such as the proof is in the pudding in formal writing
mistakes: That gave me a food for thought.
That gave me food for thought. It's uncountable: no a.
The proof is in the pudding.
The proof of the pudding is in the eating. The short form is very common in North America, but the full proverb makes the logic clear: you judge by results.
His plan is half-baked. Only baked works in this idiom.
I have a lot in my plate this month.
I have a lot on my plate. Food sits on a plate.
Don't sugar my news, just tell me.
bigidea: Lakoff and Johnson noticed that English treats ideas like food. We cook up a plan, find a theory hard to swallow, need time to digest a report, and have a taste for history. Data that hasn't been processed is raw.

The metaphor maps the whole meal onto thinking: preparing ideas (half-baked, cooked up), serving them (spoon-feed, sugar-coat), and taking them in (chew over, swallow, digest). Students who only repeat facts regurgitate them, which is not a compliment.
Because eating is so physical, these idioms are vivid and often evaluative. A meaty argument has substance; a half-baked one does not.
hidden: I need a few days to digest all this information.
It's a meaty report with plenty to discuss.
We have the raw data, but nobody has analysed it yet.
They cooked up a plan to surprise their parents.
Don't just regurgitate the textbook. Tell me what you think.
She developed a taste for politics at university.
I'm still trying to swallow the idea that he's retiring.
The documentary left a bitter taste in my mouth.

expressions.example: The speaker's comments on loneliness gave us all food for thought.
expressions.bend: Uncountable: give someone food for thought, plenty of food for thought, real food for thought.
expressions.note: Polite and positive. In a meeting, That's food for thought can also be a diplomatic way of saying I'm not convinced yet.

expressions.meaning: (of an idea or plan) not properly thought out
expressions.example: The council's half-baked parking scheme lasted three weeks.
expressions.bend: Adjective before a noun (a half-baked idea) or after be (the plan is half-baked). Fixed: always baked.
expressions.note: Quite critical. To soften, say it needs more work or it isn't fully developed yet.

expressions.example: The news that the clinic would close was hard to swallow.
expressions.bend: Also difficult to swallow, a bitter pill to swallow, or the verb alone: I can't swallow that excuse.
expressions.note: Can mean emotionally painful (bad news) or not believable (a weak excuse). Context decides.

expressions.meaning: think about something carefully before deciding
expressions.example: It's a generous offer, but let me chew it over this weekend.
expressions.bend: Separable: chew over the offer / chew it over. Also chew on it.
expressions.note: Friendly and informal. In formal writing use consider or reflect on.

expressions.meaning: make bad news sound better than it really is
expressions.example: Please don't sugar-coat it, doctor. How serious is it?
expressions.bend: A verb: sugar-coat the truth, a sugar-coated version. Often negative: I won't sugar-coat this.
expressions.note: Like a sweet coating on a bitter pill. Compare sweeten the deal, which means adding a real benefit.

expressions.meaning: give people information so simply that they don't have to think
expressions.example: University lecturers won't spoon-feed you the way some high-school teachers do.
expressions.bend: Spoon-feed someone or spoon-feed information to someone; past tense spoon-fed.
expressions.note: Critical of both sides: the teacher who over-helps and the learner who waits to be fed.

expressions.e: have a lot on your plate
expressions.meaning: have many tasks or problems to deal with
expressions.example: With a new baby and a house move, they have a lot on their plate.
expressions.bend: Have too much / enough on your plate; with everything on her plate.
expressions.note: A sympathetic way to explain why someone is busy or stressed. British speakers also say have a lot on.

expressions.meaning: offer a useful skill, idea or resource
expressions.example: Her years in Nunavut bring a valuable perspective to the table.
expressions.bend: Name the thing: bring experience/energy/a fresh perspective to the table. Question: What do you bring to the table?
expressions.note: Very common in job interviews and business. Can sound like jargon if repeated.

culture.how: Cleopatra looks back on her earlier romance with Julius Caesar and dismisses it as belonging to her salad days, when she was young, inexperienced and as green as fresh leaves. Shakespeare coined the phrase, which now means a carefree and naive youth.
culture.ask: What were your salad days like? What did you believe then that makes you smile now?
culture.find: salad days Shakespeare Antony and Cleopatra meaning

culture.how: A hungry fox fails to reach a bunch of grapes and walks away telling himself they were probably sour anyway. The fable gave English sour grapes: pretending you never wanted something you couldn't have.
culture.ask: Can you think of a public figure or company whose criticism looked like sour grapes?
culture.find: Aesop The Fox and the Grapes sour grapes

culture.how: Hughes asks what happens to a dream that is put off for too long, and imagines it spoiling like food: drying up like a raisin in the sun, festering, going rotten. The dream is food that has been left uneaten. The poem gave Lorraine Hansberry the title of her 1959 play A Raisin in the Sun.
culture.ask: What happens to a dream or plan that is postponed for years? Is food a good metaphor for it?

culture.how: The Birmingham reggae band's first single takes the idiom as its title, but the song is about real hunger: it contrasts Christmas feasting in rich countries with famine elsewhere. The double meaning makes listeners think about literal food and thought at the same time.
culture.ask: Why might a songwriter choose an idiom with a literal meaning that matches the song's subject?

match.why: Like a cake taken out of the oven too soon.
Your mind refuses it, as your throat refuses something unpleasant.
You take time, as you do when you chew slowly.
Like the sweet coating on a bitter pill.

match.r: make things too easy for learners
match.why: Like feeding a baby who can't use a spoon yet.

match.l: have a lot on your plate
match.r: have many things to deal with
match.why: Your plate is full, so you can't take more.
Like bringing a dish to share at a meal.

sort.h: Sort the expressions: are they about thinking an idea through, an idea that is not ready or not good, or serving ideas to others?

items.why: You think about it slowly and carefully.
You take time to understand it fully.
Something that gives you plenty to think about.
You read it eagerly and fast.
The idea was taken out of the oven too soon.
Information that hasn't been processed yet.
Old ideas reheated and served again.
You present bad news as sweeter than it is.
You give information in tiny, easy portions.
You present or offer something, often to an audience.
You repeat facts without understanding or adding anything.

pick.q: The guest lecture on aging gave the nursing students plenty of ___.
pick.why: Something worth thinking about = food for thought.

pick.q: The minister announced a ___ scheme to cut wait times with no funding and no staff.
pick.why: A plan with no thought behind it is half-baked.

pick.why: Painful and difficult to accept = hard to swallow.

pick.q: I'm not saying no. Let me ___ and call you on Monday.
pick.why: Asking for time to think = chew it over.

pick.q: I won't ___: the company lost money every month this year.

Let's not give Priya the extra project; she ___ already.

spot.q: The film about climate refugees gave me a food for thought.
spot.why: Uncountable: no article before food for thought.

spot.q: The mayor's half-cooked plan to ban cars downtown was dropped within a week.
spot.why: Only baked works: a half-baked plan.

spot.q: With two jobs and a sick parent, Marco has a lot in his plate.
spot.why: Food sits on a plate: have a lot on your plate.

spot.q: The doctor didn't sugar the diagnosis; she told me exactly what to expect.
spot.why: The verb is sugar-coat. Sweeten the deal means add a benefit.

spot.q: What exactly will you bring on the table if we hire you?
spot.why: You bring something to the table, like a dish to a shared meal.

type.q: The report is full of ___ for thought about rural health care.
type.why: Food for thought: something worth thinking about.

type.q: Honestly, the whole marketing strategy seems half-___ to me.
Losing the final in overtime was a bitter pill to ___.
type.why: A bitter pill to swallow: something painful you must accept.

type.q: Take a few days to ___ it over before you sign the contract.
type.why: Chew it over: think carefully before deciding.

type.q: Good teachers don't ___-feed their students; they make them think.
type.why: Spoon-feed: make learning so easy that no thinking is needed.

type.q: Her criticism of the winning design was just sour ___.
type.why: Sour grapes: criticising what you couldn't have. From Aesop.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural after an interesting talk? ___
opts: That gives us plenty of food for thought.
That gives us plenty of foods for thought.
That gives us plenty of food for thinking.
bend.why: Food for thought is uncountable and fixed, but plenty of or real can go before it.

bend.q: Which version is a natural variation of hard to swallow? ___
opts: The price rise was a bitter pill to swallow.
The price rise was a hard pill of swallowing.
The price rise was swallowing hard.
bend.why: A bitter pill to swallow is a common extended form of the same image.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural with a pronoun? ___
opts: I'll chew over it and get back to you.
I'll chew it over and get back to you.
I'll chew it and get back over to you.
bend.why: With a pronoun, separable phrasal verbs split: chew it over.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural in a job interview? ___
opts: I bring ten years of sales experience to the table.
I bring to the table of sales ten years.
I table ten years of sales experience.
bend.why: Bring + the contribution + to the table. Table as a verb means something else.

talk: Langston Hughes compares a postponed dream to food left too long. Describe a dream or plan that you or someone you know put off. What happened to it?
Is it ever right to sugar-coat bad news? Think about doctors, teachers, parents and politicians.
Role-play: you are interviewing for a job you really want. Explain what you bring to the table and ask for time to chew over the offer.
Do schools today spoon-feed students, or do they push them to think? Compare with your own education.
Describe your salad days. Where were you, and what did you believe about the world?

match.r: pretending not to want what you couldn't get
match.why: From Aesop's fox, who decided the grapes he couldn't reach were sour.
Coined by Shakespeare in Antony and Cleopatra. Green like salad.

match.l: the proof of the pudding is in the eating
match.r: you judge something by its results
match.why: Proof once meant test: you test a pudding by eating it.
Dismissive: the idea needed more time in the oven.
Critical: the learner never has to think.

spot.q: His complaints about the winner sound like sour apples to me.

spot.q: I don't want to spoon-eat you, so try the first problem on your own.

type.q: The theory sounds fine, but the proof of the ___ is in the eating.
type.why: Judge by results. Proof meant test.

type.q: When we were young and broke in Toronto, those were our salad ___.

type.q: The candidate who lost called the vote rigged, but most people saw it as sour ___.

type.q: Don't sugar-___ it. Did we get the grant or not?

type.q: Let me chew ___ your proposal over the weekend.

bank.q: Each volunteer ___, whether it's cooking, driving or just a friendly face.

bank.q: The minister's ___-baked reforms were withdrawn after a month.
bank.why: Half-baked: not properly thought out.

bank.q: You'll need time to ___ all this information; it's a lot.
bank.why: Digest information: take time to understand it.

bank.q: Calling the prize meaningless after losing it is just sour ___.
bank.why: Sour grapes: pretending you didn't want it.

bank.q: Don't just ___ the lecture notes; tell me what you think.
bank.why: Regurgitate: repeat without understanding.

bank.q: That essay on housing gave me a lot of food for ___.

bank.q: With exams and a part-time job, my daughter has a lot in her plate.
